result.summary:
Most of the lesson checks out. The implement and code-review claims match the pinned SKILL.md files and Matt Pocock's /implement article: commit to the current branch without asking, `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD`, review before commit. The GitHub docs claims match the docs: three-dot diffs in pull requests, the default squash message, and revoking a leaked secret first. Brad Traversy's `feature:` matches the transcript at about 18:57, and his gist uses `ci:`, `test:` and `feat:`. The Conventional Commits and Pro Git points are right. The Try it runs cleanly from the `recipes` repo made in What Git and GitHub are. Every /learn link points at a lesson that covers what this one promises (worktrees, the real .gitignore, squash merges, moving a commit off main). The validator prints ok, and there are no private-project or old-site leftovers.

The real problems, most of them confirmed with real Git and npm:
- Adding the missing `.gitignore` line doesn't untrack an already committed `.env.local`, so the replacement key leaks the same way. A scratch test confirmed this.
- `npm ci` fails only when `package.json` changed without the lockfile. When only the lockfile changed, it passes, on both npm 10 and npm 11.
- The hunk-header checkpoint has a wrong option, "Four lines were added", that can actually be true.

The rest are low-severity consistency, output and clarity points:
- The intro's branch size contradicts the stat.
- The cooking-time commit is put on the search branch, but the branch's own stat doesn't include it.
- Commit IDs are reused with different messages and parents from What Git and GitHub are.
- The `git status` paths are shown in the wrong order.
- The `cat-file` output is trimmed but not marked as trimmed.
- One Try it step says one line starts with `+` when two do.
- The lesson doesn't say that two dots mean something different in `git log`.
- The cheat sheet's squash rule drops the one-commit case.
- "Skill" and "fixed point" are never explained.
- One checkpoint prompt doesn't say the agent committed.

I read the whole lesson and checked every claim, command, question and link. I ran its commands with Git 2.43 against a local bare repo standing in for GitHub. The Try it output, the push and no-upstream messages, the fast-forward pull, ahead/behind/diverged, the refused pushes and `git branch -vv` all match. The format validator passes (9 final-test questions, 13 checkpoints) and there are no leftovers (no private names, no old-site features, no numbered references, no dates). Every /learn link points at a lesson that covers the topic, except the Try it's pointer to Opening a pull request. The Matt Pocock claims match the snapshot: issue-tracker-github.md's fork check, git-guardrails blocking every `git push`, and the v1.3.2 changelog's report of Issues filed in the wrong repo.

Flagged claims about this lesson, all confirmed:
- (a) `gh auth login`: this lesson's wording matches the prompt "Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?" (gh git_credential.go:63, and GitHub's "Caching your GitHub credentials" page), and choosing SSH really offers to make and upload a key. Not this lesson's problem: since gh v2.103.0 the "How would you like to authenticate GitHub CLI?" prompt comes before the protocol prompt (login_flow.go:98 vs :124; it was the other way round through v2.102.0). So what-git-and-github-are's "Pick HTTPS… Then choose to log in with a web browser" lists the prompts in the old order.
- (b) Git for Windows does install Git Credential Manager (GCM): it is the installer's default credential helper, and it signs in through the browser.
- (c) `gh repo fork X --clone` creates the fork, clones it as `origin`, adds `upstream`, makes `upstream` gh's default repo and fetches it (fork.go:363-391). `gh repo clone` of a fork also makes the parent the default. `gh repo view` picks its repo the same way as `gh issue create` (root.go:163-173), so the lesson's check works.
- (d) The github.com details (Code button, + menu, Fork button and Owner menu, Sync fork, Update branch conditions, branch menu) match GitHub Docs. The branches-and-worktrees `-d` claim isn't in this lesson.
- Also checked: the Pro Git quote is exact, VS Code's Sync Changes does pull then push, the Forks reference page says a fork "has its own settings", and `gh repo create --source=. --push` runs `git push --set-upstream origin HEAD`.
- Note, not a finding: current Git docs call `ls-remote --heads` a deprecated synonym for `--branches`. But `--branches` fails on Git 2.43 (Ubuntu 24.04), so keep `--heads`.

Problems: 5 medium, 6 low (details below).
